newsitem.title: USA: Two dead, eight missing after U.S. plane crash.
newsitem.headline: Two dead, eight missing after U.S. plane crash.

text.p: Searchers rescued one survivor but two airmen were dead and eight were missing after a U.S. Air Force Reserve transport plane plunged into the Pacific Ocean, officials said on Saturday.

Coast Guard Petty Officer Jeff Murphy said searchers scouring the area around the crash site off the northern California coast had recovered two bodies after pulling one survivor from the water on Friday night.

No more survivors have been found despite an intensive search by military and civilian planes and ships, but officials said there was still hope and the search was continuing. "We have located survival gear and rafts. There's always a chance they climbed into it," Murphy said.

The HC-130 Hercules with 11 airmen on board crashed about 60 miles (95 kms) off Cape Mendocino on the northern California coast on Friday evening after reporting engine and electrical problems. Debris was scattered over a wide area.
Two Coast Guard cutters were involved in the search and a third was on the way, Murphy said. A Navy destroyer, a merchant ship and a fishing boat were also helping.

The Air Force and Coast Guard have sent a total of four helicopters and two C-130s to the scene, Murphy said. The Air Force said it was convening a board of officers to investigate the cause of the accident.

With visibility of 12 miles (20 kms) and short, choppy seas, search conditions were described as adequate as long as daylight lasted. Searchers were scouring a huge 108 square mile (280 sq km) area for possible survivors, Coast Guard spokesman Chief Petty Officer Ronald Cabral said.

"They should find something today," Cabral said earlier on Saturday. He said "there's always hope" of finding more survivors. Other officials said hypothermia was a danger for anyone spending that long in the cold water.

The hulking four-engined aircraft, a military workhorse, was flying from Portland Air Base to San Diego, California on a routine training mission when crew members reported they had shut down one engine and also had electrical problems, Air Force spokeswoman Karole Scott said from Portland, where the plane was based. Soon afterwards, air traffic controllers in Oakland and Seattle lost radar and radio contact, she said.
Coast Guard Lt. Joe Pesci said the crew had told authorities it planned to turn toward land for a precautionary landing just before contact was lost.

The rescued airman, Technical Sgt. Robert Vogel, a 31-year-old airborne communications specialist from Albany, Oregon, was flown to a California hospital where he was listed in stable condition, the Air Force said.
Scott said the families of the crew members had all been notified in person that they were missing. "They are being supported by our officers," she said.
The plane was assigned to the 939th Rescue Wing's 304th Rescue Squadron, the Air Force said. In war time, the unit's mission is combat rescue behind enemy lines, Scott said.
